Orwell is- as the name implies- a government surveillance simulator.  You are an operator of the new titular system Orwell, and you are told to help the government of The Nation to catch a terrorist.  As the plot unfolds, you find yourself having to increasingly question what you're doing, and whether the ends- catching actual murderers- justify the means, the lies, and the rights you've violated to get there.

As you process information on your targets, you find related documents to the info you're processing.  Now and then this proves finnicky, with some documents unlocked in a manner very reminiscent of a Point-and-click adventure game's "How does THAT make sense?!" moments.  In addition, while the story has a great deal of branching going on (with choices being made based on what data you choose to process and which of pairs of conflicting data you choose to work with), many of the points it tries to bring up fall hollow as some of the very, very evil people you deal with try to decry the bad you've done to catch them.  Imagine if Hitler had been captured by the Allies, and on the stand in Nuremberg said "Okay, so yeah, I genocided a LOT of people and that was probably wrong, but I HAD to; the Treaty of Versailles was inexcusable!"  Much like one is not inclined to listen to Hitler's points about the morality of excessive punitive measures in war treaties, the end of Orwell leaves you less than immersed and willing to concern the finer points of the game's questions on the morality of government surveillance, largely due to the person presenting the final decision.

All of that aside, however, this game gets a very firm recommendation.  It was a deep and interesting game, and despite being shot in the foot by some despicable characters (in among some very good and well-written ones) it still managed to raise thought-provoking questions on how far is too far for a government to go to catch criminals.

A decent narrative experience about mass surveillance.

Your task is seemingly simple: uncover the truth behind the Freedom Plaza bombing. In order to achieve this, you will traverse blogs, read social media and eavesdrop on people's calls. Every bit of information (here called "chunk") may be helpful to determine who was the perpetrator all along.

Well, of course it would not be [i]that[/i] easy. More and more people appear to be involved, more and more information is conflicting, meaning you have to decide which data you will input into the eponymous Orwell system (and *when* will you input them) for the government to act on.

While your actions will have consequences, this is still a linear experience.

If you are a fan of such games, why not giving it a try?

Note: I [b]DO NOT[/b] recommend the sequel, which is a far shorter game and does not provide enough novelties to be worth your attention. Stick to this one.

[b]tl;dr:[/b] The description doesn't make clear that this is a visual novel. Don't expect much decision making, or even actual deduction--[i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] holds your hand throughout the experience. If you can forgive that, and stomach the occasionally doubleplusungood prose, you'll have a decent (if predictable) exploration of surveillance. Modestly recommended; only buy during sales.

-

It's the World Of Tomorrow™, and an enigmatic nation known only as, well, The Nation is preparing the implementation of an as of yet unannounced surveillance program. With the Orwell AI on your side, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a terrorist attack, so that the government can prove the efficacy of the program and rally the support of the public. But things are not as they seem, and what was supposed to be a simple case quickly spirals out of control.

Actual gameplay, if it can be called that, mostly consists of diving into the digital lives of target persons. Now and then, the AI will highlight processable pieces of information, which are known as datachunks. If you feed a datachunk to the system, it will be sent to a government advisor on the other end of the line, who can then use the evidence to justify an arrest, call in a special ops team, et cetera. Because the advisor only gets to see those datachunks that you choose to process, he can't really read the information in its proper context, allowing you to paint a misleading picture through selectivity. By (ab)using this indirect influence, you can steer the turn of events into your preferred direction.

The idea sounds interesting enough on paper, and admittedly, it sometimes is--when the game is at its best, your choices really [i]do[/i] feel as if they matter. More often than not, though, you just go down a funnel, with your advisor telling you what to do for every step of the way. Events are supposed to happen in real-time, but are actually tied to your storyline progress; after something significant has happened, events will usually grind to a halt until you've passed some checkpoint. This implementation strips the concept of much of its strength, and it would be nice if Osmotic Studios had been a tad bit more honest about this. Indeed, I went in with a much more sandboxy expectation. Buyer, beware: [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a glorified visual novel, with no real interaction beyond some scripted points of divergence. I don't think that is necessarily a bad thing. I [i]do[/i] think it is important to know.

Another thing that cheapens the experience is the implausible interface of the AI. From time to time, you will encounter two contradictory datachunks, but instead of doing the sensible thing (uploading them both for later review), the AI will [i]force[/i] you to make a choice, even if you don't have nearly enough context to do so informedly. For some reason, these uploads can't be reversed if you find better information down the road. Even more questionably, the AI can somehow [i]know[/i] that a certain datachunk will contradict with another, even if the contradicting datachunk hasn't been found yet! I understand that these things are necessary for gameplay purposes--calling the shots in solving contradictions is one of the key ways to manipulate your advisor--but they really do shatter one's immersion.

So far, I have been pretty negative about this game, so you might be wondering why I still recommend it. The reason is quite simple: the story, is well worth experiencing. Characters feel like real, actual people who could be living next door, not like empty robots who are just there to advance the plot. And it is the very lack of meaningful choice that allowed the writers to go this far: most games are wide but shallow, [i]Orwell[/i] is narrow but deep. Granted, the attempts to make the player question their own morality mostly fall flat (contrary to what the reviewer consensus seems to be, good and evil are clear from the start), and the social commentary that permeates the writing has a distinct feeling of 'heard it all before'. There is also an overreliance on deus ex machina, particularly near the end of the story. But the characters and their various interactions are captivating enough to make you genuinely care about their fates. You might even find yourself on the edge of your seat, even though you never get to see the action directly. In my opinion, that more than makes up for the cheap plot devices, as well as the [i]very[/i] variable quality of the prose. The many references to George Orwell's [i]Nineteen Eighty-Four[/i] add to the charm.

In short, [i]Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You[/i] is a mediocre game, but with a respectable narrative. As long as you keep your expectations in check, it will certainly provide an afternoon of entertainment.

It works as social commentary, but the game is not really about investigating, since you have to act more on guesses and gut feelings than on facts.
[spoiler]The system is used to find people to blame, instead of being used to guide more conventional investigations, so your guesses are taken as facts, your bits of data are taken as the whole picture, and they are used to lock people up (or get them killed!).[/spoiler]

[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

I don't have a lot of games by steam hoarder standards (a little less than 500), but sometimes I stumble upon games in my library that I wasn't even aware I had. This was the case with Orwell, and I'm glad that I found this hidden gem.

Gameplay wise Orwell is an episodic, point and click, interactive visual novel, in a dystopian future, with interesting questions regarding freedom, privacy, security and the pros and cons of the digital era. As a researcher you have to use Orwell (a complex governmental surveillance system) to investigate the lives of multiple citizens of the fictional country "The Nation", and find out those responsible for a series of terror attacks. You can do this by listening to phone calls, reading blog posts, and personal e-mails, hacking laptops, phones and going through medical files, bank records etc. As you make your connections and draw your conclusions you can tailor the story here and there, and you can decide who to incriminate or who to help, but overall your choices do not define the final outcome of the game that much. I liked the atmoshpere and the story has some interesting twists, plus there are multiple endings so it has some replay value as well. Good job Osmotic Studios, this was a very enjoyable experience.

I was happy to find out that there is a sequel to Orwell, I'll definitely buy it in the upcoming months!

There aren't many games I would be willing to write a review for but this game far exceeded any expectations I had, so I feel like it's important other people play. I went into this thinking it would be a fun little simulation of figuring out a terrorist attack but it quickly descended into a twisting crossroads of privacy, guilt, lies, and what it means to be safe. Plus it was really fun reading over all the info to try and find clues about what's true, what's a false flag, and how to manipulate things just the right way.

Orwell is a unique concept that keeps you digging for the entire time.

You play as a government investigator of The Nation, using the Orwell system to collect information about people who pose potential threats to The Party.

It pulls heavy inspiration from George Orwell's 1984, and you'll notice it right off the bat, with your advisor going by the name "Symes".

It's a short game, and to 100% it, you won't need more than 7-8 hours, but I really feel like it's worth your time. It gives a scary, realistic insight about a path down to an Orwellean future, where everything you say and do is on display for the government.

Not outright bad, as I still enjoyed playing the game, but especially at the end pretty unsubtle and ham handed.  Very timely game that reflects our time though,

Didn't work for me. Not as a game.
It was an okay-interesting story, but the game played itself. I never had to think, just drag some highlighted text from the right to the left. And when the game actually put me in a situation where I had to think, by giving me the choice between two hypotheses, it did so with too little information. It felt especially bad because the game is fake-real-time, meaning things happen "as time goes by", but really only the game progresses as you take actions. So what would almost always happen was that (literally) immediately after submitted your hypothesis - your guess - as a FACT, the game goes "oh, this just in! Here's the information you could have used to make a sound judgement, if you'd just waited to click send for 5 seconds!". You continuously felt like an absolute impatient amateur switching between doing monkey work gathering information and then posting your guesses as facts to a board. And why can't I then write them and say "Hey, I just got this information! You know that thing I said earlier? Yeah, something has come up, and that is now completely wrong!" Absolutely destroyed my immersion.
All in all, the game just made me more and more annoyed, as the focus was more on "gut-feeling" than "deduction" (and maybe there's some social commentary on that. I never got it). In the end, the game feels more like a visual novel with tacked on interactive elements - more than it feels like an immersive story where you feel like an Orwellian observer and manipulator.

Thanks to the recent sale on narrative games and my watching Oreimo for the first time (Do not ask about the correlation) I decided to pick up this game as there is little more fascinating to me than dystopian scenarios and a good mystery story - which is of course what we have right here otherwise I wouldn't be talking about it.

While I am not one to preach about privacy issues in real society this game offers a powerful insight into where things go wrong, even when it seems all the necessary precautions are being made to keep privacy invasion to a minimum. The core concept sees you working for the government of a fictitious foreign nation which has introduced numerous security systems and laws in order to reduce crime levels. While this is all well and good in theory it fails to stop a terrorist attack taking place in plain view of the entire nation. Your task - and there is no choice but to accept it - is to investigate the suspicious individuals linked with these attacks by searching through their social media, medical documents, online dating accounts - literally any source of digital information in which small chunks of information can be uploaded to the government in order to draw conclusions.

What those conclusions are however is often up to you, while the game does a very good job of using all its various information sources to lead you to the right chunks of data conflicts do arise. When a chunk of data contradicts with another it is up to you to decide which side of the argument you wish to submit. You can draw a conclusion quickly, or use all the information at your disposal to logically determine which is correct - simple though it sounds there are instances where no amount of logic will lead to the answer, the choice is then left to your conscience, and which choice you believe is the right one to make. Take note that the game makes no attempt to hide the fact that you are affecting real (fictional) lives and the implications of your actions will very quickly become apparent - People will almost certainly die because of things that you have done, or that you did not do.

Before I continue rambling about the core concept of this game and how powerful it is and how exciting it is to slowly unravel the mystery at the heart of things though, I do have to comment on probably the one thing that really stood out to me  - [b]Sound[/b]
Yes it is weird to comment about how powerful sound is when you play a 6 hour game that for almost its entirety is the same slow jingle of ambient generic "We are a megacorporation" music, there was never a point in the game where i wasn't drastically unsettled by the sudden, VERY powerful changes in this music that occurred the few times where a huge piece of key information is displayed on the screen for the first time. Your eyes might not even be there yet, you might still be reading the paragraph above and just preemptively scrolled the page down already but BOOM, the music plays, something big is right there in front of you, highlighted in blue and in plain view. Your eyes aren't there yet but you know it is there. You want to finish reading the paragraph above for full context, but it's right there. You know it is there. You must look. You must.

TL;DR: Powerful game, intriguing mystery afoot, definitely recommend, please play with sound

[b]Guys!  Perhaps this may come as a shock to some of you but, in case you didn’t know, this game has a bit of an agenda….[/b] 
Ok ok, joking aside I bought Orwell a while back when it fell below my “if I buy this and don’t like it, I won’t feel any great loss” threshold.  It sat in my library untouched until a rainy day when I didn’t feel like getting into anything too involved.  I say this to admit that I went into this with pretty bland expectations.  

I generally view games like this the way I do a book from an unknown author, but that has a premise I like.  I knew going in that the game makers had a point to make and even though it was a point I generally agree with, I was a little wary.  [i]I don’t like being preached at, so I wasn’t sure if I was going to spend the entire game being beat over the head with the rhetoric bat whilst being presented with billboards saying in big bold letters “Hey look, the authors feel very strongly about this” at every turn or if the game would have any merit beyond the political statement.[/i]  [b]I’m very thankful to say that this game was far more than just a tray upon which to serve political and social commentary and it was even very clever in doing so.[/b]

So why did I start out with all that waffle about political commentary?  Because I want to set the tone for how I approached the game and the preconceptions I had going in.  I went into the experience thinking that I pretty much had them figured out and that I would easily be able to see through any “hard choices with lasting consequences” to what the authors were really trying to sell to the player.  And chapter 1 pretty much was just that.  I “knew” they were trying to get me to suspect a particular person and that they wanted me to assume the simple answer so they could jump out from behind the posterized, low-polygon trees and say “Ha!  See how even with all the information at your fingertips you jumped to the wrong conclusion.”  So naturally I did just the opposite.  Purposefully ignoring what I assumed were red-herrings and by the end of chapter 1, I’d almost lost interest figuring that I had it all figured out.  I was delighted, and a bit disappointed, that I was wrong.  

Starting chapter 2, I was actually engaged in the narrative and was now determined not to be caught off-guard again.  I still knew there was a point to it all, but I wasn’t as sure I knew what that point was.  By the end of the game, I knew what was going on, but because I’d fed information to orwell earlier on that seemed harmless at the time, I’d built a profile on some of the characters that was not incorrect but was misrepresentative.  This led to events playing out in a way that I didn’t want and with no way to go back and correct.  I felt duped, but in a good way.  The game had indeed gotten it’s point across, but in a very subtle and engaging way that left me still feeling that I enjoyed the experience.

So let’s sum this up, shall we? 
•	Orwell was well worth the money
•	Gameplay was not nearly as on-rails as I had expected
•	Story was actually very engaging and believable
•	Plot twists did not feel super-contrived simply to force the player to be wrong for the sake of proving a point.  All the plot twists could have been seen coming I think if the user had paid attention to the details and not just focused on what Orwell highlights.
•	The game actually made me think and didn’t preach it’s point smugly from contrived moral high-ground and I appreciated that.  

Here is where I would usually list a few things that could have been improved, but the game is pretty simple and the UI layout is simple and easy to use.  Some of the “websites” that you visit have clickable links that aren’t obvious… that was kind of annoying, but not too bad.  I’d like to say that I wish you could go back and edit information when you found out it was wrong, but I think it’s integral to the game the concept that YOU are the filter.  If it’s not relevant, accurate, or then you don’t upload it.  If I had one complaint it would be that I sometimes didn’t know what would “trigger” the next event and so sometimes I’d upload something I didn’t really want to just because I thought I had to in order to progress the game.   

All in all, the game took me about 6 hours to play through… you could go longer or shorter, but in the end, it’s not a great investment timewise…. In fact, it practically gives you a good stopping point between chapters.  I highly recommend the game.  It’s worth $7-10 for your time and as a good conversation starter.  Gift it to a friend so you can have a good conversation on the topic.  

Anyway, That’s my 2 cents worth.

-John

I mean, we're basically living in a world where we're being tracked and viewed as corporate commodities, so this game isn't much of a stretch. Still, I found myself really enjoying Orwell - so much so that I purchased the next game in the series (Ignorance is Strength) shortly after completing it. The basic premise behind Orwell is that you're an investigator snooping on your fellow citizens in order to connect the dots behind a larger conspiracy. Your choices, of course, will have an impact on the game's ending; they'll also decide the fate of individual characters - whether they escape, get arrested, or even die. The storyline is interesting and presents you with a lot of ethical dilemmas; things are never black and white, although you can certainly make some intriguing choices trying to adhere to such a worldview.

Overall, I don't have many complaints about the game itself. The UI is pretty slick and easy to navigate. Music is nice. However, I wish there was a way to easily skip/speed through phone calls and such. If you want to unlock every achievement, then you'll need to play through the game 3 or 4 times; having the ability to skip or speed through certain dialogues/events would make that feel less cumbersome. I mean, it's worthwhile to replay the game just to see what happens when you make different choices or approach situations from another perspective; it can just feel a bit tedious when you're looking for a specific achievement.

As an added bonus, the second game in the series (Orwell: Ignorance is Strength) takes the events of the first game into consideration. You can even import your investigator's decisions, allowing you to relive the events of the first game while playing through the second. I won't spoil anything, but I like that the developer made that decision; it ties the games together nicely. I'd recommend this game for fans of the cyberpunk/dystopian genres, especially - you'll definitely appreciate the themes and overall feel of the game.

Fun game that gives you a lot to think about. 7/10

Good things:
- Loved the story and its themes. Ethics were not black and white, but rather very nuanced.
- Loved the game mechanics. Yes, it's a simple drag and drop game, but the beauty is in this simplicity.
- Loved the realism. Characters seemed like real people who can make mistakes, make jokes, panic, and lie.

Bad things:
- Calls and text conversations tend to be slow and are not able to be skipped.
- I had to play the whole game three times to get all achievements. Although, there was a bit more to learn each time, it was still very boring.

I loved the game mechanic, which was utterly innovative. I loved the headline feature as it helped with worldbuilding and let you know about storyline events. The plot was solid and I loved the way the plot twists slowly unfolded. The characters were well fleshed-out as well.

 I will say there's limited replay value and because of that the game felt a little short. Additionally, unless it was simply the way I played, everyone suspected WAS guilty in some form. You were technically right in getting the police involved each time. I would have liked to see a point where you got someone who was tangentially involved (like one of the people running the cybercafe) be arrested/interrogated etc. Since the idea is that suspicion is enough to assume guilt, having an innocent person be suspected would have helped prove the point of the system's wrongness. That's mostly nitpicking though, and not a huge issue. 

Additionally, since you generally had to choose specific data chunks to advance the story it limited your ability to alter the plot. Which, it's an authoritarian regime so if you didn't give the required information that would likely turn out badly for you- but that also adds to the lack of replay value. If there was more alternative routes I would definitely play through each, so I'm just a little disappointed that I can't do so.

I don't think replay value is the only thing that determines whether a game is good, and this one certainly left an impression. I highly recommend it and I'll definitely be getting the sequel somewhere down the line.
